Testing With Imputation

Group 2

DATA COLLECTION

set.seed(12)

data <- read.csv("../Video_Games_Sales_as_at_22_Dec_2016.csv",sep=",",na.strings=c(""," ","NA","N/A"))

data_row_count <- nrow(data)

Number of rows = 16719

# Show data
datatable(data[1:6,], 
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 6),
          rownames = FALSE)

DATA CLEANSING

# Drop all sales except global
data_df <- cbind(data[,-c(6:10)],data$Global_Sales)
data_df$Year_of_Release <- 2016 - data_df$Year_of_Release
names(data_df)[3] <- "Game_Age"
names(data_df)[12] <- "Global_Sales"

data_df <- data_df %>% mutate(User_Score = as.numeric(na_if(User_Score, "tbd")))
data_df$User_Score <- data_df$User_Score * 10

#name column is an id column we can remove for good (only used for games Top ten sales)
data_df <- data_df[,-1]

str(data_df)

DATA IMPUTATION (Bayesian Linear Regression)

keep_columns <- c("Global_Sales", "Platform", "Game_Age", "Genre", "Critic_Score", "Critic_Count", "User_Score", "User_Count", "Rating")

# Overwrite the data with only those columns
data_subset <- data_df[, keep_columns]

data_subset$Platform <- as.factor(data_subset$Platform)
data_subset$Genre <- as.factor(data_subset$Genre)
data_subset$Rating <- as.factor(data_subset$Rating)

# Bayesian Linear Regression
#meth <- make.method(data_subset)
#imp_data <- mice(data_subset, method = meth, m = 5, seed = 123, printFlag = FALSE)

imp_data <- mice(data_subset, 
                    method = "pmm", 
                    m = 1,           # Keep m=1 for speed during drafting
                    maxit = 5,       # Standard iterations
                    seed = 123, 
                    printFlag = FALSE)

completed_data <- complete(imp_data, 1)

datatable(completed_data[,-c(6:10)], 
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 6),
          rownames = FALSE)

REGRESSION MODEL

set.seed(12)

reg_model <- completed_data
str(reg_model)

train.size <- floor(0.7*nrow(reg_model))
train.index <- sample(1:nrow(reg_model),train.size, replace = F)
train.set <- reg_model[train.index,]
test.set <- reg_model[-train.index,]

DIAGNOSTIC CHECKING

I. NORMALITY

1. Graphical Analysis of Residuals

qqnorm(residuals(model), ylab="Residuals")
qqline(residuals(model)) # Normality using Q-Q Plots

2. Statistical Test

Ho: ϵ’s normally distributed.

Ha: ϵ’s not normally distributed.

2.1. Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test
resid_std <- scale(residuals(model)) # mean=0, sd=1
ks_test <- ks.test(resid_std, "pnorm") # Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test
ks_test
## 
##  Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
## 
## data:  resid_std
## D = 0.24295, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: two-sided

We reject the null hypothesis, therefore, the residuals are not normally distributed.

II. HOMOSCEDASTICITY

1. Graphical Analysis of Residuals

plot(fitted(model), residuals(model))

2. Statistical Test

Ho: Heteroscedasticity is not present.

Ha: Heteroscedasticity is present.

2.1. Breusch-Pagan-Godfrey Test
bp_test <- bptest(model) # Breusch-Pagan test
bp_test
## 
##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  model
## BP = 189.84, df = 53, p-value < 2.2e-16

We reject the null hypothesis, therefore, Heteroscedasticity is present.

III. MULTICOLINEARITY

1. Statistical Test

vif_values = vif(model)
vif_values
##                   GVIF Df GVIF^(1/(2*Df))
## Platform     17.985716 30        1.049338
## Game_Age      7.337145  1        2.708717
## Genre         2.718300 11        1.046504
## Critic_Score  2.098707  1        1.448691
## Critic_Count  1.886678  1        1.373564
## User_Score    1.879333  1        1.370888
## User_Count    1.309692  1        1.144418
## Rating        2.265242  7        1.060145

VIF > 5 -> moderate concern

VIF > 10 -> serious multicollinearity

## [1] "Rating is okay (VIF = 1.06 )"

IV. INDEPENDENCE

1. Graphical Analysis of Residuals

n = length(residuals(model))
plot(tail(residuals(model), n-1) ~
head(residuals(model), n-1),
xlab=expression(hat(epsilon)[i]),
ylab=expression(hat(epsilon)[i+1]))
abline(h=0, v=0, col = grey(0.5))

2. Statistical Test

Ho: No auto-correlation (the errors are uncorrelated)

Ha: There exists auto-correlation

2.1. Durbin-Watson Test
dw_test = dwtest(model) # Durbin-Watson Test
dw_test
## 
##  Durbin-Watson test
## 
## data:  model
## DW = 0.40758, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is greater than 0

We reject the null hypothesis, therefore, there exists auto-correlation.

DATA TRANSFORMATION (Logarithmic Model)

Since the model is not normally distributed based on the results of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, we perform a data transformation using the Logarithmic Model.

train.set$Log_Global_Sales <- log(train.set$Global_Sales)

model_log <- lm(Log_Global_Sales ~ Platform + Game_Age + Genre + Critic_Score + Critic_Count + User_Score + User_Count + Rating, data = train.set)

summary(model_log)

DIAGNOSTIC CHECKING AFTER DATA TRANSFORMATION

I. NORMALITY

1. Graphical Analysis of Residuals

qqnorm(residuals(model_log), ylab="Residuals")
qqline(residuals(model_log)) # Normality using Q-Q Plots

2. Statistical Test

Ho: ϵ’s normally distributed.

Ha: ϵ’s not normally distributed.

2.1. Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test
resid_std <- scale(residuals(model_log)) # mean=0, sd=1
ks_test <- ks.test(resid_std, "pnorm") # Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test
ks_test
## 
##  Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
## 
## data:  resid_std
## D = 0.010405, p-value = 0.1586
## alternative hypothesis: two-sided

We fail to reject the null hypothesis, therefore, the residuals are normally distributed.

II. HOMOSCEDASTICITY

1. Graphical Analysis of Residuals

plot(fitted(model_log), residuals(model_log))

2. Statistical Test

Ho: Heteroscedasticity is not present.

Ha: Heteroscedasticity is present.

2.1. Breusch-Pagan-Godfrey Test
bp_test <- bptest(model_log) # Breusch-Pagan test
bp_test
## 
##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  model_log
## BP = 491.24, df = 53, p-value < 2.2e-16

We reject the null hypothesis, therefore, Heteroscedasticity is present.

III. MULTICOLINEARITY

1. Statistical Test

vif_values = vif(model_log)
vif_values
##                   GVIF Df GVIF^(1/(2*Df))
## Platform     18.725192 30        1.050043
## Game_Age      7.558729  1        2.749314
## Genre         2.718971 11        1.046515
## Critic_Score  2.096231  1        1.447837
## Critic_Count  1.885766  1        1.373232
## User_Score    1.873463  1        1.368745
## User_Count    1.315425  1        1.146920
## Rating        2.278522  7        1.060588

VIF > 5 -> moderate concern

VIF > 10 -> serious multicollinearity

## [1] "Platform is okay (VIF = 1.05 )"

## [1] "Genre is okay (VIF = 1.05 )"

## [1] "Critic_Count is okay (VIF = 1.37 )"
## [1] "User_Score is okay (VIF = 1.37 )"
## [1] "User_Count is okay (VIF = 1.15 )"
## [1] "Rating is okay (VIF = 1.06 )"

IV. INDEPENDENCE

1. Graphical Analysis of Residuals

n = length(residuals(model_log))
plot(tail(residuals(model_log), n-1) ~
head(residuals(model_log), n-1),
xlab=expression(hat(epsilon)[i]),
ylab=expression(hat(epsilon)[i+1]))
abline(h=0, v=0, col = grey(0.5))

2. Statistical Test

Ho: No auto-correlation (the errors are uncorrelated)

Ha: There exists auto-correlation

2.1. Durbin-Watson Test
dw_test = dwtest(model_log) # Durbin-Watson Test
dw_test
## 
##  Durbin-Watson test
## 
## data:  model_log
## DW = 2.019, p-value = 0.8482
## alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is greater than 0

We fail to reject the null hypothesis, therefore, there is no auto-correlation.
